newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Secret Small Business.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Secret Small Business.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV political correspondent)
"Unless you can develop a plan to get small business going again ... you haven't got a snowflake in hell's chance of reducing youth unemployment."
That was one of John Howard's great election pitches delivered in the febrile atmosphere of his first "great" debate with Paul Keating during the 1996 election campaign.

Rhetoric is one thing, reality is quite another, particularly when it comes to small business and Howard's pledge to the shopkeepers of the nation is proving quite a headache for the prime minister and his government.
For years, shopping centre tenants and franchisees have been complaining about the onerous and unfair behaviour of shopping centre owners and franchisors.

Whether on rents or the terms of the franchise or whatever, small business people believe big business has them over a barrel and take every advantage of what they regard as unfair opportunities to exploit them.
Economic rationalists might say it's simply the market at work, but as the recent car tariff decision demonstrated, politics is often mightier than the market.
Particularly when Howard has made such a great show of his concern for small business and what he says is its role in job generation.
Trouble is -- despite all the prime minister's jawboning since his election -- unemployment remains higher than Labor left it.
More seriously, small business has won precious few concessions from the government beyond cuts to the provisional tax uplift factor and easing for capital gains tax rollover provisions.
Paul Keating tried to argue before his defeat that Howard's expressed concern for small business was a smokescreen -- that the Liberals and had always been the party of big business.
For evidence, Keating pointed to the coalition's frustration in the Senate of Labor's legislation supposed to make life easier for franchisees.
In fact, he strived to make it an election issue.

But the voters had other things on the mind -- it was not a subject they were about to take on board during the five weeks of the election campaign when they'd already decided to take the baseball bat to the ALP.
Now the boot's on the other foot and Howard's small business credentials are facing a severe test.
The issue is the parliamentary report into fair trading and Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser's carriage of it.
Prosser owns three shopping centres in Western Australian and is landlord to some 80 tenants.

How, mutter small business representatives, can they be sure of a fair outcome with the report in the hands of a man whose own business interests are at odds with theirs -- regardless of whether he's a good landlord or not.
Labor thinks this is fertile ground -- and not just because Prosser is a shaky and unconvincing parliamentary performer.
The minister denies he's in breach of the prime minister's code of conduct even though it indicates a minister should not be involved in decisions in an area where he has business interests.

Despite the denial, Prosser effectively admitted he was on shifting sands by stating that if there were any "perceived" conflict of interest about the report it would be handled by Industry Minister John Moore.
The opposition has yet to land anything like a killer blow, but has drawn enough blood to make it clear Prosser is compromised.

Not only does the small business community now know that the minister owns three shopping centres, but that he has at least 80 tenants, among them franchisees -- the very subject of the report of which he has carriage.

Further, Prosser has been in contact with Coles Myer director Nick Greiner on behalf, he says, of his brother. The minister insists it had nothing to do with his portfolio and was not a breach of John Howard's code of ministerial conduct.
But the code does declare that a minister should not be involved in the day to day running of his business -- and such an approach is sailing very close to the wind on that score.
At least one of Prosser's tenants had also revealed that the minister's shopping centre manager regularly contacts "Geoff" over business details -- again sailing close to the wind.
Looking ahead, it would seem likely Prosser will absent himself when cabinet makes a decision on the fair trading report. It also seems likely cabinet will reject its recommendations.
That would open the way for Labor to declare it an unfair decision promoted by a biased minister.
All ammunition for the opposition during the next election campaign when it strives to hive off some of the key small business support which Howard attracted in 1996.
